phil-eth-01-c2.text: Richard Joyce (2021). Moral Anti-Realism. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
phil-eth-01-c2.quote: there is no such property, or at least nothing in the world instantiates it
phil-eth-01-c2.claim: Error theory (Mackie) holds that moral statements aim to describe objective facts, but no such facts exist, so all positive moral claims are false.

phil-eth-01-c3.text: Rachel Cohon (2018). Hume's Moral Philosophy. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
phil-eth-01-c3.quote: proceeding in the ordinary way of reasoning, at some point make an unremarked transition from premises whose parts are linked only by 'is' to conclusions whose parts are linked by 'ought.'
phil-eth-01-c3.claim: David Hume noticed that moral arguments often slip from statements of fact ('is') to statements of obligation ('ought') without justification.

phil-eth-01-c3.text: van Roojen, Mark (2004). Moral Cognitivism vs. Non-Cognitivism. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
phil-eth-01-c3.quote: According to Hume’s Law, no set of premises consisting entirely of non-moral descriptive statements is sufficient to entail a moral or normative conclusion.
phil-eth-01-c3.claim: This is now called Hume's Law: you cannot derive moral conclusions from purely natural facts without additional moral premises.

phil-eth-03-c1.text: Johnson, Robert, Cureton, Adam (2004). Kant’s Moral Philosophy. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
phil-eth-03-c1.quote: Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) argued that the supreme principle of morality is a principle of rationality that he dubbed the “Categorical Imperative” (CI).
phil-eth-03-c1.claim: Immanuel Kant argued that morality is grounded in reason, not consequences.

phil-eth-05-c1.text: McIntyre, Alison (2004). Doctrine of Double Effect. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
phil-eth-05-c1.quote: (examples from Thomson, 1985, based on examples in Foot 1967).
phil-eth-05-c1.claim: Judith Jarvis Thomson's trolley problem (1985) and Philippa Foot's original (1967) have become the paradigm of applied moral thought-experiment.

phil-eth-05-c2.text: Nelkin, Dana K (2004). Moral Luck. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
phil-eth-05-c2.quote: All of those who accept the existence of some type of moral luck reject the Control Principle and the Kantian conception of morality that embraces it.
phil-eth-05-c2.claim: Moral luck creates tension with the Kantian intuition that moral worth depends only on what is within your control.
